content: Behavioral definitions of violence against women (VAW), including marital rape, should align with international human rights standards and normative frameworks. By capturing data on sexual violence and the relationship between the survivor and perpetrator, a minimum data set can identify instances of sexual violence committed by spouses. While sectors like police and justice may not record non-criminalized forms of VAW, health and social services can utilize the minimum data set to document such cases. Country experiences show that in the absence of prevalence surveys, administrative data can effectively raise awareness among policymakers about VAW and drive improvements in policies and programs. Recording all forms of VAW using behavioral definitions aims to make these forms more visible and recognized by survivors and service providers, ultimately leading to better laws, policies, and programs. However, cultural norms and legal definitions influence what types of VAW are reported and recorded, with less recognized or non-criminalized forms being significantly underreported. However, multiple visits by survivors to different services do not constitute double counting. Addressing these concerns is crucial for improving data literacy among policymakers and data users. Ideally, service delivery sites should identify new and repeat users in their information systems to report the number of survivors and perpetrators interacting with services over a specific period. This requires a unique identifier, which may be used within a single service site or across multiple services and sectors. Identifying the number of VAW case reports, survivors, and perpetrators at each stage of institutional processes is essential for building a comprehensive framework that facilitates cooperation between relevant agencies. Databases with unique identifiers can link data across sectors, providing insights into VAW interventions and outcomes. For example, linked data between health and police services can analyze how many women received referrals in both directions, accessed forensic services, or had cases that progressed to court and resulted in convictions. Argentina’s Unified Registry of Cases of Violence Against Women (RUCVM) demonstrates the value of using case reports as the unit of count while also providing the option to collect unique identifiers for survivors. This registry collects a minimum data set, including survivor demographics, relationship to the perpetrator, type and frequency of violence, and services provided. In 2018, 57% of registered cases included a unique survivor identifier, enabling additional analyses, such as determining that 81% of survivors with unique identifiers had only one contact with a service provider. Kosovo’s integrated database for VAW, established under its National Strategy for Protection Against Domestic Violence, collects information on VAW and institutional responses. Housed in the Ministry of Justice, the database uses the individual (survivor or perpetrator) as the unit of count and tracks cases through the system, including referrals and services provided. Training and support for institutions and personnel are critical for effective VAW data collection and management. Training should emphasize the importance of VAW data collection in achieving national and sectoral priorities, while also addressing privacy, confidentiality, and survivor safety. Multidisciplinary training teams, including VAW experts, data management specialists, and survivor representatives, can enhance the capacity of service providers to collect and manage VAW data empathetically and respectfully. Implementation plans for VAW administrative data collection should include training and resource planning, recognizing that capacity building requires ongoing efforts. Training should provide practical opportunities for data collection and entry, emphasizing survivor consent and confidentiality. For example, in India, WHO’s training of healthcare providers significantly improved their ability to identify and support survivors of violence, document cases, and provide appropriate referrals and care. Standard operating procedures (SOPs) for data management, including secure storage and access protocols, are essential to maintain data quality and confidentiality.
